title: What is mindfulness?
citation: Maddock, A., & Blair, C. (2023). How do mindfulness-based programmes improve anxiety, depression and psychological distress? A systematic review. Current Psychology, 42(12), 10200-10222.
content:
What is mindfulness?

Mindfulness is the practice of paying attention to the present moment with openness and curiosity, rather than judging or trying to change what you notice. It involves becoming aware of your thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations and surroundings as they are happening. Instead of getting caught up in the past or worrying about the future, mindfulness helps you bring your attention back to what is happening right now.

Isn't mindfulness just clearing your mind of all thoughts?

A common misconception is that mindfulness means having a completely empty mind. In reality, the goal is not to stop thoughts but to notice them without becoming carried away by them. Thoughts will naturally come and go. Mindfulness teaches you to recognise them, allow them to pass and gently return your attention to the present, whether that is your breathing, your body, or your surroundings.

Why does mindfulness help with stress and anxiety?

When we are stressed or anxious, the mind often becomes stuck in cycles of worry, rumination, or imagining future problems. Mindfulness helps interrupt these patterns by shifting attention away from automatic thinking and back to the present moment. Practising mindfulness also activates the body's relaxation response, helping to slow breathing, reduce muscle tension and calm the nervous system. Over time, this can make it easier to respond thoughtfully rather than react automatically to stressful situations.

What does being present actually feel like?

Being present does not mean feeling calm all the time or having no thoughts. Instead, it often feels like being more aware of what is happening in the moment without immediately judging it or trying to change it. You may notice the sensation of your feet on the ground, the rhythm of your breathing, or the sounds around you. Thoughts and emotions may still be there, but they no longer have to completely pull your attention away from what you are doing.

Mindfulness vs relaxation: what's the difference?

Although mindfulness can feel relaxing, relaxation is not its main goal. Relaxation focuses on reducing tension and creating a sense of calm. Mindfulness is about increasing awareness of your experience, whether it feels pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. Sometimes mindfulness feels calming, while at other times it simply helps you notice difficult thoughts or emotions with greater acceptance. The aim is to change your relationship with your experiences rather than trying to make them disappear.

Why does my mind wander so much when I try to focus?

It is completely normal for the mind to wander during mindfulness practice. The brain naturally shifts between memories, future plans and distractions. This happens to everyone. In fact, noticing that your mind has wandered is an important part of mindfulness. Each time you gently bring your attention back to the present, you are strengthening the skill of attention, much like exercising a muscle. A wandering mind is not a sign that you are doing mindfulness incorrectly.

How do I start mindfulness practice?

Mindfulness does not require long meditation sessions or special equipment. Many people begin by spending just a few minutes each day focusing on their breathing, noticing sensations in their body, or paying full attention to an everyday activity such as drinking tea or taking a walk. Like any skill, mindfulness becomes easier with regular practice. Doing it consistently can help build greater awareness, improve emotional regulation and reduce the impact of stress over time.
